# APWG Phishing Activity Trends Report, 1st Quarter 2026: original summary

This file is an original, source-grounded summary of the identified APWG report, not a reproduction of the copyrighted report.

The Anti-Phishing Working Group published its first-quarter 2026 Phishing Activity Trends Report on May 21, 2026. It covers activity from January through March 2026 and draws on reports from APWG member companies, research partners, the public reporting website, and email submissions. APWG distinguishes unique phishing sites from individual URLs, tracks distinct phishing email subjects as a rough measure of lure variety, and normalizes brand names when counting targeted brands.

APWG reported 971,181 phishing attacks in Q1 2026, up 13.8 percent from 853,244 in Q4 2025. It identified 766 unique targeted brands during the quarter. Telecom was the most-targeted sector at 33 percent, followed by SaaS/webmail at 20 percent. APWG also reported growth in telephone-based fraud and described impersonation and scams as the dominant threat categories observed on social platforms. The report cautions that email-system blocking can reduce the number of lure messages forwarded to APWG, affecting one of its collection channels.

The APWG trends page has since published a Q2 2026 summary. This file intentionally represents the specifically identified Q1 2026 report and its publication date; it does not extrapolate its figures to later quarters.

# Using Caution with Email Attachments

This file is a condensed, source-grounded adaptation of the official CISA page, not a verbatim copy of the complete page.

This CISA page is archived and warns that archived information may not reflect current policy or programs.

## Why can email attachments be dangerous?

Some characteristics that make email attachments convenient and popular also make them a common tool for attackers. Email is easily circulated, almost any type of file can be attached, and some email programs automatically download attachments. Attackers can spoof return addresses, so a message that appears to come from someone familiar is not necessarily legitimate.

## Steps to protect yourself and others

- Be wary of unsolicited attachments, even from people you know. If possible, confirm with the supposed sender before opening an attachment. Internet service providers and software vendors do not send patches or software in email.
- Keep software up to date and enable automatic operating-system updates when available.
- Trust your instincts. Do not open a suspicious email or attachment merely because antivirus software says it is clean; new malware may not yet have a known signature.
- If an attachment must be opened before its source can be verified, update antivirus signatures, save the file, manually scan it, and open it only if it is clean and does not seem suspicious.
- Turn off automatic attachment downloads.
- Consider reading email using an account with restricted privileges rather than administrator privileges.
- Apply additional security practices, such as filtering certain attachment types through email software or a firewall.

# Phishing Guidance: Stopping the Attack Cycle at Phase One

This file is a condensed, source-grounded adaptation of selected passages from the official joint guidance PDF, not a verbatim copy of the complete document.

## Overview

Social engineering is the attempt to trick someone into revealing information (e.g., a password) or taking an action that can be used to compromise systems or networks. Phishing is a form of social engineering where malicious actors lure victims (typically via email) to visit a malicious site or deceive them into providing login credentials. Malicious actors primarily leverage phishing for obtaining login credentials and malware deployment.

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), National Security Agency (NSA), Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), and Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center (MS-ISAC) released this joint guide to outline phishing techniques malicious actors commonly use and to provide guidance for both network defenders and software manufacturers. The guide includes tailored recommendations for small- and medium-sized businesses and secure-by-design and secure-by-default guidance for software manufacturers.

## Selected mitigations for organizations

- Implement user training on social engineering and phishing attacks. Regularly educate users on identifying suspicious emails and links, not interacting with suspicious items, and reporting instances of opening suspicious emails, links, attachments, or other potential lures.
- Enable Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC) for received email, together with Sender Policy Framework (SPF) and DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM), and set DMARC to reject for sent email.
- Implement internal mail and messaging monitoring and scrutinize deviations from normal traffic.
- Harden credentials with FIDO or PKI-based multi-factor authentication. Prioritize phishing-resistant MFA for administrators and privileged users. If mobile push MFA cannot be replaced, use number matching to mitigate

internal mail and messaging monitoring and scrutinize deviations from normal traffic.
- Harden credentials with FIDO or PKI-based multi-factor authentication. Prioritize phishing-resistant MFA for administrators and privileged users. If mobile push MFA cannot be replaced, use number matching to mitigate MFA fatigue.
- Incorporate denylists at the email gateway and firewall to block known malicious domains, URLs, IP addresses, high-risk extensions, and mislabeled extensions.
- Restrict administrative rights, apply least privilege, use application allowlists, and block macros by default.
- For small and medium-sized organizations, prioritize annual phishing-awareness training, strong MFA, DNS filtering or firewall denylists, anti-virus protection, high-risk file restrictions, automatic software updates, and safe-browsing policies.

## Incident response

If phishing compromises credentials or executes malware, the guide says to re-provision affected accounts, audit account access, isolate affected workstations to prevent spread, and have the malware analyzed. It also directs organizations to report phishing incidents through the appropriate channels.

# Google: How to spot scams, and what to do if you encounter one — original summary

This file is an original, source-grounded summary of Google’s October 2, 2024 article, not a reproduction of the copyrighted article. It is the exact article corresponding to the project document’s shorthand description “How to spot email, phone, text and web scams.”

Google advises treating unexpected messages and urgent requests for sensitive or financial information with suspicion. For email, verify the actual sender address rather than trusting its display name, watch for lookalike domains, inspect link destinations before clicking, and ignore password-reset messages you did not request. Spelling or formatting errors can still be warning signs, although polished language does not prove a message is safe.

For calls and texts, ask questions without volunteering information, avoid links and app downloads sent by unknown people, and never share temporary passwords, passcodes, or two-step verification information. Urgency is a warning sign. Use built-in spam warnings, but independently verify a caller or sender through contact information obtained from an official source.

On the web, inspect unfamiliar URLs before opening them, investigate advertisers and businesses using authoritative sources, and be cautious with unusual formatting or unofficial customer-service details. If scammed, change passwords, check whether account details were altered, contact banks and linked accounts, enable stronger protections such as passkeys and two-step verification, and report the crime to the appropriate authorities.

# NIST Phish Scale User Guide (TN 2276): original summary

This file is an original, source-grounded summary rather than a reproduction of the NIST Phish Scale or its worksheets.

NIST Technical Note 2276 describes the Phish Scale as a method for phishing-awareness training implementers to rate how difficult a simulated phishing email is for a person to detect. The guide is meant to add context to exercise click rates: results should be interpreted alongside the difficulty of the message, rather than assuming every simulated message posed the same detection challenge. NIST says the method considers characteristics of the email and the user context of its recipient. The publication includes instructions for applying the method, worksheets, and supporting discussion of email properties and related research.

The publication page identifies the final document date as November 15, 2023 and provides DOI 10.6028/NIST.TN.2276. NIST’s current Human-Centered Cybersecurity page adds an important licensing condition: academic use is available at no cost, but organizations must establish a research license agreement with NIST; commercial applications require a commercialization license. Consult NIST’s Technology Partnerships Office before applying or redistributing the method. This summary does not reproduce the scoring method or worksheets.

# Phishing

You were just going about your day, managing your small business when you realize you can no longer log in to your bank account. Did you forget your password or has someone changed the log in, effectively blocking you from your own money? Were you “phished”?

## What is Phishing?

Phishing is the use of convincing emails or other messages to trick us into opening harmful links or downloading malicious software. These messages are often disguised as a trusted source, such as your bank, credit card company, or even a leader within your own business.

## How to Spot a Phish

Artificial intelligence (AI) can now be used to craft increasingly convincing phishing attacks, so it is more imperative than ever to take a second, or third, look at any message requesting you to take action—such asking you to click a link, download a file, transfer funds, log into an account, or submit sensitive information. What to look out for:

- A request to download an attachment or click on a link– treat all attachments and links with caution.
- A sense of urgency. They want you to act now. Stop and take a moment to think about the request. Verify the request by using known contact information or information from a public company website, not from the message itself. Or if you get an urgent message from your boss or a vendor, contact them directly to verify the message.
- Suspicious looking source email address. Would your bank email from Chase@gmail.com?
- A request for sensitive information, like bank account information or Social Security number.

## How Can I Protect My Business from Phishing?

- Teach employees how to spot and report a phish when they have fallen victim or think they have fallen victim to a phishing attack.
- Recognize that email isn’t the only way to get phished. You can also receive attacks through text messages, phone calls, social media messages, or even physical postal mail.

- Don’t engage with the sender, and do not click any link in the email (including unsubscribe). Just delete the message. You can report phishing crimes to the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center.
- Deploy and maintain anti-virus software – if the phishing attack aims to install malware on your computer, up-to-date anti-virus software may help prevent the malware from installing.
- Utilize email filters – many email services have configurable filters that can help prevent many phishing messages from ever reaching your employees’ mailboxes.
- Configure email security technologies – email services can also implement email authentication technologies that verify where messages originated and can reject messages that are spoofed. Check with your provider to see what security options are available.
- Enable multi-factor authentication. Take it to the next level by implementing phishing-resistant authentication.

## What should I do if I think I’ve been a victim of a phishing attack?

- Change any affected passwords – If possible, immediately change the password for any affected accounts. If this password was also used for other online accounts, change the passwords for those accounts to something unique and strong.
- Contact the fraud department of the breached account – If the phishing attack compromised your company’s account at a financial institution, contact the bank immediately to report the incident. Monitor for unauthorized transactions to the account. If a personal account was involved, contact the 3 major credit bureaus to enable fraud alerts.

immediately to report the incident. Monitor for unauthorized transactions to the account. If a personal account was involved, contact the 3 major credit bureaus to enable fraud alerts.
- Notify appropriate people in your company – follow your company’s incident response plan to ensure the appropriate personnel are aware of the incident.
- Notify affected parties – if personal data of others (e.g., customers, suppliers) was compromised, be sure to notify them. The compromised personal data could be used for identity theft. Check the website of your state’s attorney general for information on data breach notification requirements.

## Questions to Consider

- Do our employees know how to spot a phish?
- Are we regularly training employees to raise their awareness of phishing threats?
- Do our employees know how to report if they think they have fallen victim to a phishing attack?
- Is multi-factor authentication (MFA) required and used on all accounts that offer it? Especially accounts that access sensitive information? Are we using phishing-resistant MFA?
- Are we regularly updating our business technologies and software when updates are available?

# Unvalidated Redirects and Forwards Cheat Sheet

This is an attributed, lightly condensed adaptation of the OWASP Cheat Sheet under CC BY-SA 4.0, not a verbatim copy of the complete page.

## Introduction

Unvalidated redirects and forwards are possible when a web application accepts untrusted input that could cause the web application to redirect the request to a URL contained within untrusted input. By modifying untrusted URL input to a malicious site, an attacker may successfully launch a phishing scam and steal user credentials.

Because the server name in the modified link is identical to the original site, phishing attempts may have a more trustworthy appearance. Unvalidated redirect and forward attacks can also be used to maliciously craft a URL that would pass the application's access control check and then forward the attacker to privileged functions that they would normally not be able to access.

## Preventing Unvalidated Redirects and Forwards

Safe use of redirects and forwards can be done in a number of ways:

- Simply avoid using redirects and forwards.
- If used, do not allow the URL as user input for the destination.
- Where possible, have the user provide a short name, ID, or token which is mapped server-side to a full target URL. Be careful that this does not introduce an enumeration vulnerability.
- If user input cannot be avoided, ensure that the supplied value is valid, appropriate for the application, and authorized for the user.
- For local return URLs, use a framework helper that rejects non-local destinations.
- If external destinations are required, allow-list explicitly approved destinations using parsed URL components.
- Force redirects through a page that tells users they are leaving the site, clearly displays the destination, and asks them to confirm.
